extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, journalism students, and ethics committees
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for investigating newsroom ethical breaches and reforming hiring, supervision, and editorial policies after a credibility-damaging scandal. Focuses on committee composition, stakeholder engagement, responsibility assignment, verification practices, and accountability measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative investigative committee membership
rubrics_metrics.description: The consequences of Blair’s actions are so broad that it is important to have representatives from all staff levels, as well as journalists outside the Times staff, weigh in on corrective steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include voices from all levels of the newsroom (junior to senior) and invite independent journalists or professionals outside the organization to ensure diverse perspectives and credibility. This broad representation helps surface systemic causes and builds trust in remedial recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership by highly ethical consensus-builders
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading this group should be one or several highly ethical consensus-builders who can solicit and synthesize ideas from throughout the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose leaders with strong ethical reputations and facilitation skills rather than partisans or close insiders; they should be able to solicit input widely and forge broadly acceptable reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad stakeholder identification and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders range from the humble retiree who simply reads his paper in the morning to the power-wielding diplomat who relies on foreign-policy reports to inform her decisions. As a group, biggest stakeholders are citizens of democracies, which depend on journalists to grow trust in readers with accurate reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating damage and designing reforms, consider the varied public and institutional audiences affected (readers, policymakers, other journalists) and how trust-restoration measures will be perceived across these groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine hiring, management and editorial policy for systemic causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Blair case raises questions about hiring, management and overall editorial policy. First, there is the issue of relative inexperience in a super-high-stakes newsroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit recruitment and promotion practices to determine whether rapid advancement of inexperienced staff or insufficient mentorship/supervision contributed to ethical breakdowns. Assess whether talent was privileged over necessary experience and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign responsibility for oversight failures across editorial hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it the editor who hired him straight from the University of Maryland? How about successive editors, who, despite their mediocre evaluations, did not object loudly enough to Blair’s promotions? Could the executive and managing editors, with their big-picture roles and busy days, truly be responsible for one staffer’s malfeasance?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should identify where supervisory lapses occurred at hiring, supervisory, and executive levels and recommend accountability measures or process changes that address those specific failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider use of an outsider auditor vs insider leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it enough to know what went wrong and tighten the reigns on practices such as anonymous sources? Or does the Times need an auditor, someone it pays for a scolding? Why should an outsider be allowed to make recommendations on better internal practices? Then again, how could an insider, in earshot of the mess itself, lead the committee to fix things?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh pros and cons of hiring an external reviewer (for impartial recommendations) versus relying on insiders (who know institutional context). The Times’ response combined an insider-led inquiry that recommended hiring an outsider (Daniel Okrent) for further improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission both insider and outsider review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times decided that to remedy the nasty ramifications of the Blair scandal, it would commission an insider, along with others in and outside the Times newsroom, to investigate problems and suggest changes. The insider, Siegal, decided the Times should hire an outsider (who would be former Life magazine editor Daniel Okrent) to suggest further improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A two-tier review (internal committee to gather facts + independent external reviewer to evaluate and recommend reforms) can combine institutional knowledge with impartial critique and public credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tighten verification practices, especially regarding anonymous sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Times editorial policy changed to reflect a much more cautious, conservative atmosphere concerning staff promotions and, especially, verification of reporting. A notable example of the latter aspect regards anonymous sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform editorial standards to strengthen fact-checking and verification protocols, limit or more strictly vet anonymous sourcing, and codify expectations for corroboration before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement formal performance documentation for transfers/promotions
rubrics_metrics.description: In terms of staffing, the Times went so far as to require written evaluations for any candidates transferring between posts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require documented written evaluations and clear criteria for promotions or transfers to ensure that personnel decisions rest on verifiable performance and supervision records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbolic accountability to help restore institutional credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A particularly difficult aspect of the fallout, although one welcome by staffers who felt marginalized, was the dual resignation of Raines and Boyd. That development, at least in the view of Publisher Arthur Sulzberger, was for the greater good of the Times. Symbolically, their departures made it possible for observers to view the Times as a reformed institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether personnel changes (including resignations or removals at leadership levels) are necessary not only for substantive reform but also to signal accountability and help restore public trust. Balance symbolic acts with structural reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance meritocracy with required experience and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: While a pure meritocracy allows an individual of any experience level to fill any role, talent in the absence of experience could lead to diminished professionalism: Blair’s ability to impress editors with his writing may have led to him feeling that facts are less important than prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design hiring and promotion systems that value both demonstrated talent and sufficient experience/supervision; implement mentorship, fact-verification oversight, and clear expectations so that strong prose does not substitute for factual rigor.
